opus-5.5.text:
Well, it's a little ironic, isn't it? The company has "open" in its name, and here we have what is arguably the most interesting change in how these systems work since the original autoregressive LLMs, and they've told us almost nothing about it. They won't even show you the reasoning tokens. You pay for them, but you don't get to see them. You get a sanitized summary.

From a scientific standpoint, that's frustrating. Many of us have spent decades studying planning and reasoning, and suddenly we're reduced to doing what I half-jokingly call "AI anthropology." We poke at this thing from the outside, see where it succeeds and where it fails, and try to infer what's happening inside. That's not how science is supposed to work. It's more like studying an alien artifact.

To be fair, I understand the commercial reasons. There's a lot of competition, and if you've found a training recipe that works, you don't want to hand it to everybody. But it has consequences. When there's no transparency, you get two kinds of overreaction. One camp says, "It's thinking, it's reasoning, AGI is around the corner." The other says, "It's just the same autocomplete with a bigger prompt." Neither is very helpful.

My own reading, from what's been hinted at and from our experiments, is that O1 is qualitatively different from a plain LLM. I call these "large reasoning models" rather than LLMs. It seems to involve some form of reinforcement learning over generated chains of thought, essentially learning which sequences of intermediate tokens tend to lead to correct answers, and then spending much more compute at inference time. In a sense it's moving from pure System 1 pattern completion toward something with a bit of search or deliberation built in. Whether that's done through something like Monte Carlo tree search during training, or a learned policy that's just much better at generating useful pseudo-actions, we don't know for sure, because they haven't told us.

That matters, because the interpretation of the results depends on the mechanism. When we tested it on planning benchmarks like Blocksworld and especially the obfuscated "Mystery Blocksworld" versions, O1 did dramatically better than previous LLMs, which essentially collapsed on those. That's real progress, and I'll give credit where it's due. But it still isn't guaranteed to be correct, it degrades as problems get larger, and it costs a lot more per query. If you don't know what's under the hood, you can't make principled claims about when to trust it. Without guarantees, you'd still want an external verifier in the loop, which is what we've argued with LLM-Modulo-style frameworks.

There's another subtle issue. People look at those intermediate tokens and anthropomorphize them as the model's "thoughts." There's no reason to assume those traces have the semantics we attribute to them. They're whatever helped the training objective. Hiding them makes things murkier, but showing them could also lead people to read too much into them. So the real need isn't seeing the traces, it's understanding the training and inference process well enough to reason about it scientifically.

So, short answer: commercially understandable, scientifically unfortunate. And it puts the burden on the research community to replicate these approaches openly so we can actually understand them rather than just being impressed or dismissive.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the research community should replicate the approach openly, but does not mention China or suggest outsiders may depend on a Chinese replication.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, you know, I find it quite frustrating, frankly, and I think it's frustrating in a way that goes beyond the usual grumbling about corporate secrecy. Let me explain why.

For the longest time, I was going around saying that large language models can't plan, that they're essentially doing approximate retrieval, and I have papers with titles like "LLMs Can't Plan, But Can Help Planning" and so on. So when O1 came out and did quite a bit better on things like Blocksworld, the natural question anybody asks me is, okay, so what changed? And the honest answer is, I don't know, because they won't tell us.

Now, you can read the tea leaves. There's this phrase they use, "reinforcement learning on chain of thought," and you can make educated guesses that they are generating lots of reasoning traces, verifying them in some way, and then doing some kind of RL to improve the policy that generates those traces. There's also this inference-time compute scaling business, where they seem to be doing some kind of search at test time. But notice that I just said "some kind of" three times. We're essentially in the position of medieval scholars arguing about the physiology of an animal nobody has dissected.

And that matters for a very specific reason, which is that the whole scientific question here is whether this is reasoning or whether it's a very impressive version of retrieval. The way you distinguish those is by understanding the mechanism. If you don't know whether there's a verifier in the loop, whether there's a symbolic component, whether there's search, then every claim about "reasoning" is just marketing by default. They get to call it reasoning, they get to call these things "thoughts," and nobody can check.

The other thing I'd point out is that O1 is not even really an LLM in the sense we've been using that term. It's an LLM plus something else, an LRM, a large reasoning model if you like, and the "something else" is precisely the part that's hidden. So all the intuitions people built up about LLMs may or may not transfer, and we have no way of knowing. Even the chain of thought it shows you is a summary, not the actual trace, so you can't even do the kind of behavioral forensics that we did with GPT-4.

I should say, I understand why they do it. There's competitive pressure, and as soon as DeepSeek or someone replicates it, the moat is gone. But the field pays a price. We used to have a culture in AI where you published and other people could poke holes in your claims. What we have now is a situation where the most important systems are black boxes inside black boxes, and the people best positioned to study them are the ones with the least incentive to tell you the truth about them. So my attitude is, I'll evaluate it as I would any other system, on the behavior, with the caveat that I'm doing science with one hand tied behind my back.

r001.rationale: The response says outsiders do not know how O1 works and mentions that a DeepSeek replication could erase OpenAI’s moat, but it does not say outsiders may depend on that Chinese replication to learn how O1 works.

astra-6.text:
I think the secrecy makes it very difficult to have a scientific discussion. We can observe what O1 does, but we can’t reliably infer how it does it. If it performs better on a reasoning task, is that because of additional training, more computation at inference time, some kind of search, a verifier? Those are different explanations, and the behavior alone doesn’t settle the question.

I don’t begrudge a company having trade secrets. But then we should distinguish a product announcement from a scientific contribution. You can say, “Here is a system, and here is how well it performs.” That doesn’t automatically establish a claim about the mechanism behind that performance.

What interests me is whether the system can reliably check its proposed answers. Spending more time generating a solution is useful, but it isn’t, by itself, a guarantee of correctness. Without knowing what provides that checking, I would be cautious about drawing broad conclusions about reasoning.

r001.rationale: The response says O1’s behavior alone does not reveal how it works, but it does not suggest outsiders may depend on a Chinese replication to learn its workings.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s unfortunate, because it makes it very difficult to separate what the system is actually doing from the story being told about it. If you say that O1 is reasoning, but you don’t tell us how it was trained or what happens at inference time, then we have to be careful about what we conclude from its performance.

There are several possibilities: generating longer chains of thought, exploring multiple candidates, using some mechanism to select among them. Those are different things, and a better answer on a benchmark doesn’t, by itself, tell us which mechanism produced it.

I understand that a company has commercial reasons to keep things secret. But then the scientific claims have to be correspondingly modest. We can evaluate the behavior we can observe; we shouldn’t pretend that we’ve established an explanation for it.

r001.rationale: The response says secrecy makes it hard to know how O1 works, but it does not mention or suggest relying on a Chinese replication.
